questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Units of Digital Memory' refers to.
questions.a: Stored data is counted in binary digits; eight of them form a byte, and bigger units such as kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte and terabyte are each 1024 times the unit just below them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Units of Digital Memory'.
questions.a: Each step up the memory ladder multiplies the capacity by 1024, so conversions chain factor after factor.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Units of Digital Memory', in plain ASCII form.
Using the method 'Bits, Nibbles and Words', work with: word_bits = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of byte_count.
questions.a: 1 bytes

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Bits, Nibbles and Words' and work with: word_bits = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of byte_count.
questions.a: 10 bytes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Bits, Nibbles and Words' refers to.
questions.a: A single binary digit is a bit; four bits grouped together make a nibble, two nibbles make a byte, and a word is the block of bits a processor handles in one go.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Bits, Nibbles and Words'.
questions.a: Grouping starts at 4 bits per nibble and 8 bits per byte, then grows to the processor's word size.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Bits, Nibbles and Words', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: byte_count = word_bits // 8

concepts.title: Data Transfer over the System Bus

questions.q: Using the method 'Data Transfer over the System Bus', work with: bus_rate_mbps = 8, file_mb = 8192. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of time_s.
questions.a: 8192 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Data Transfer over the System Bus' and work with: bus_rate_mbps = 18, file_mb = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of time_s.
Explain in your own words what 'Data Transfer over the System Bus' refers to.
questions.a: Wires that carry data, addresses and control signals between the CPU, memory and devices together form the system bus; moving a block of data takes at least its size divided by the link's transfer rate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Data Transfer over the System Bus'.
questions.a: The data bus runs both ways, while address and control buses carry information in one direction only.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Data Transfer over the System Bus', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: time_s = mbit / bus_rate_mbps

questions.q: Using the method 'Clock Speed and Instruction Throughput', work with: clock_ghz = 40, cycles_per_instr = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of instr_per_sec.

Take the relation taught for 'Clock Speed and Instruction Throughput' and work with: clock_ghz = 45, cycles_per_instr = 75. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of instr_per_sec.
Explain in your own words what 'Clock Speed and Instruction Throughput' refers to.
questions.a: An internal clock emits pacing pulses at a fixed rate; a higher clock rate or fewer cycles needed per instruction lets the processor finish more instructions every second.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Clock Speed and Instruction Throughput'.
questions.a: A gigahertz rating means billions of pacing pulses each second, which sets the pace of execution.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Clock Speed and Instruction Throughput', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: instr_per_sec = clock_ghz * 1000000000 / cycles_per_instr

questions.q: Using the method 'Moore's Law Transistor Growth', work with: base_count = 15, years = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of transistors.
Take the relation taught for 'Moore's Law Transistor Growth' and work with: base_count = 20, years = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of transistors.
Explain in your own words what 'Moore's Law Transistor Growth' refers to.
questions.a: An observation made in 1965 that the count of transistors fitted onto a single chip tends to double roughly every two years, which drives the exponential rise in computing power.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Moore's Law Transistor Growth'.
questions.a: A count that doubles every two years turns modest beginnings into astronomically dense chips within a decade.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Moore's Law Transistor Growth', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: transistors = base_count * 2 ** (years // 2)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Structured, Semi-structured and Unstructured Data' refers to.
questions.a: Records that sit in fixed rows and columns are structured; items carrying internal tags, like HTML pages or CSV files, are semi-structured; free-form media such as audio, video and photographs are unstructured.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Structured, Semi-structured and Unstructured Data'.
questions.a: Check for a rigid table format, internal tags, or neither, and that decides the data type.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Structured, Semi-structured and Unstructured Data', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: classify(source) as structured, semi-structured or unstructured

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Language Translators and Machine Code' refers to.
questions.a: A processor acts only on machine code, so source code must first be converted: assemblers handle assembly language, compilers render a whole program in one pass, and interpreters convert plus run a single line at a time.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Language Translators and Machine Code'.
questions.a: A compiled program runs afterwards without its translator, but an interpreted program needs the interpreter present on every run.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Language Translators and Machine Code', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: source code -> translator -> object code
